Everything Coming and Going on Netflix for January 2016

As a cord-cutter I've relied on Netflix for a long time. Yesterday I actually considered dropping the service for a month or two because I find that I'm watching far more Amazon Prime. I have nothing to back this up, but it sure seems like Amazon Prime's movie catalog is about 3 or 4 times the size of Netflix. Most of it is really old stuff, and often cropped to 4:3 ratio, but they seem to have a shit-ton more movies...everything from old Westerns, Film Noir, Italian gangster films, 70s sex comedies...you name it. Right now I'm watching a comedy film from the 70s called "Skateboard." I'd never heard of it, but it's a really interesting period piece. I watched a GREAT documentary called Dream Deceivers (about the Judas Priest trial in 89) the other night which was originally a PBS doc--something you'd never find on Netflix.

I don't believe they get stuff like Stanley Kubrick films (like Netflix), but they do have a fairly exhaustive catalog of HBO content. I really do enjoy Daredevil on Netflix, but it seems more and more of the "movies" they get are underwhelming and they're banking mostly on original content.

I haven't been quite as up on Amazon's catalog, but I have found myself watching far far less of Netflix with their original content push turned up to what seems like an 11. I agree that the rest of their content has felt underwhelming, and I've been considering dropping it for a while. This past year it has seemed like there's only one or two things that come up every 3 or 4 months that I feel are must-watches for me. I've been on the verge of cancelling it for some time, and this list doesn't seem to be making any strong arguments for me keeping it.

I still like Netflix streaming, but as a guy who REALLY likes old/obscure films, Amazon Prime's selection is really just awesome. The bad thing about Amazon Prime stuff, though, is that they have so much stuff it can be difficult to find what they have. The way I normally discover stuff on Amazon is hitting the "Customers also watched" icon--it'll pull up a shit-ton of stuff in the same genre. As an example, if I watch an old Basil Rathbone Sherlock Holmes movie from the 1940s, and hit "Customers also watched" it'll start showing me all the other Sherlock Holmes films in Prime, as well as Charlie Chan, Mr Moto, and shit like that. Sometimes they even have multiple copies of the same film available for streaming--I always have to check those because one might be a shit print cropped to 4:3, whereas the other might be a pristine HD restoration. It can be confusing, but I'd rather have the selection than not.

I'm not trying to bash Netflix, but they really don't seem too interested in building a bigger library. They seem to have a limited selection and just keep rotating content allowing the overall number to remain fairly static. I don't know if Amazon has a different strategy, but the sheer volume of films they have is MUCH deeper than Netflix--but the bulk of it is old stuff that most folks won't care about.

I've actually come to view them as complimentary services. Both have awesome original content (Mozart in the Jungle, Man in the High Castle on Amazon; Jessica Jones, Sense8, House of Cards on Netflix). What one lacks in movie or TV offerings the other usually can supply. Each is innovating new methods of content delivery, Amazon's video subscriptions being one I particularly like.

Even with four subscriptions (Netflix, Amazon [Curiosity Channel tacked on to Prime] & Gaia) we are still coming out money ahead versus being cable TV subscribers. Particularly in light of this news http://www.nbcnews.com/business/business-news/cable-satellite-tv-costs-will-climb-again-2016-n484531

I agree with you on them being complimentary. I've just been going to Netflix less and less. I actually ration my viewing there (e.g. half an episode a night) to justify keeping Netflix. Now when Daredevil comes back for Season 2--I'm all in. Honestly, it might be better for me to only activate Netflix every other month. I f'ing love Amazon Prime because I get free streaming music which I listen to all the time, and I can download Prime movies to my el-cheapo Amazon Fire tablet to watch them at the gym. It's just a more complete and more affordable service.

I'll never go back to cable, but of course Comcast is fucking me with data caps (I've hit mine a number of times by streaming). Since you seem to be a cord-cutter too, you should definitely check out CBS News. They've got a channel on Roku and XBox One. I watch it all the time on my computer as well. I actually really like it far better than CNN (which I no longer get) or MSNBC (which I get via the Channel Pear app on Roku).

Oh yeah, we cut the cord years back, when we went through another round of CTV price spikes that pushed us into the $200/mo. altitudes. That was just too rich for my blood. After it was all said and done, with cable internet and phone, we were back down in the $45/mo. range for the first year and I think it's hanging right near $60/mo. now.

I can also sympathize about going to Netflix less. I'm also guilty of doing the same with Amazon to a lesser degree. Especially since I discovered PLEX, which there's a ROKU app for. The server side of the application is free and dead dog easy to set up. Once that's done just point the PLEX app at your server and voila!, you can stream all of your content through your ROKU. I have audiobooks, music, movies and TV running through there all the time.

I also agree with you on the CBS News app on ROKU. There may be a day or two delay on feature pieces that aired through 60 Minutes or Sunday Morning, but that's a small price to pay to see less strident coverage of current events and noteworthy stories.

Australian government tells citizens to turn off two-factor authentication

The Australian government has repeatedly called for citizens to turn off two-factor authentication (2FA) at its main digital government portal, myGov. The portal's Twitter account has recently been updated several times with cute pictures encouraging holidaymakers to "turn off your myGov security codes" so that "you can spend more time doing the important things."

The portal is the place where Australian citizens can use and manage a number of governmental services, including health insurance, tax payments, and child support. In case of myGov, two-factor authentication is implemented by sending users text messages that contain one-time codes to complement their usual passwords.

A number of people on Twitter pointed out that, while downplaying security isn't a good idea in general, it could be even more dangerous when citizens go abroad:

.@myGovau People go into higher risk secnarios (open hotspots, internet cafes) and you suggest downgrading security? How silly /cc @troyhunt

— Tatham Oddie (@tathamoddie) December 22, 2015

The reasoning behind myGov's suggestion is understandable: some tourists will swap their Australian SIM cards to local ones while on holiday. Once this is done, they won't be able to receive myGov security codes without reinstalling their Australian SIMs, which is a hassle. Further Reading What amateurs can learn from security pros about staying safe online

Research uncovers stark differences in security practices of experts, non-experts.

While simpler for travelers, the government's suggestion guts the protections offered by two-factor authentication, which can provide an additional layer of security when logging in on the Web. 2FA is even more important when you're not on a trusted home or office network, which is why the Australian government's recommendation to turn off 2FA is rather jarring.

In the wake of criticism from users for the unsafe advice, myGov posted on Twitter that people who turn off security codes will "still need to securely sign in with secret questions & answers." The tweet offers a link to read more on the possibility, however the page it leads to doesn't mention it.

Even if it did though, a few additional passwords aren't a true replacement for good ol' two-factor authentication.

This post originated on Ars Technica UK
